cards.title: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes
cards.prompt: A patient's morning labs show K+ 6.8 with peaked T waves on ECG. What do you do first?
facts: Give IV calcium gluconate immediately to stabilize the cardiac membrane, then start insulin with dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly, and add a beta-agonist nebulizer. Kayexalate/patiromer or dialysis handle total-body potassium removal afterward.
cards.pearl: Calcium doesn't lower potassium — it protects the heart while the other therapies get to work.
cards.explanation: Give IV calcium gluconate immediately to stabilize the cardiac membrane, then start insulin with dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly, and add a beta-agonist nebulizer. Kayexalate/patiromer or dialysis handle total-body potassium removal afterward.

cards.title: DKA resolution vs. glucose normalization
cards.prompt: Your DKA patient's glucose is now 140 but the anion gap is still 18. Do you stop the insulin drip?
facts: No — add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion until the anion gap closes. Stopping insulin early risks a ketoacidosis rebound.
cards.pearl: Anion gap closure, not glucose, is the true endpoint of DKA treatment.
cards.explanation: No — add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion until the anion gap closes. Stopping insulin early risks a ketoacidosis rebound.

cards.title: Schistocytes and thrombocytopenia
cards.prompt: Peripheral smear shows schistocytes and platelets are 38,000. Do you transfuse platelets?
facts: Hold platelet transfusion unless there is life-threatening bleeding. Send ADAMTS13 and call hematology urgently for consideration of plasma exchange.
cards.pearl: In TTP, platelet transfusion can fuel further microthrombi rather than help.
cards.explanation: Hold platelet transfusion unless there is life-threatening bleeding. Send ADAMTS13 and call hematology urgently for consideration of plasma exchange.

cards.title: Working a high anion gap
cards.prompt: A patient's anion gap comes back at 24. What's your next step?
facts: Work through the differential (methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, iron/INH, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates) and order a lactate, ketones, osmolar gap, and toxicology screen based on the clinical picture rather than everything reflexively.
cards.pearl: The differential is a checklist for your next order, not just a list to recite on rounds.
cards.explanation: Work through the differential (methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, iron/INH, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates) and order a lactate, ketones, osmolar gap, and toxicology screen based on the clinical picture rather than everything reflexively.

cards.title: Painless jaundice work-up
cards.prompt: A patient presents with painless jaundice and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. Do you manage this like gallstone disease?
facts: No — this is Courvoisier's sign. Pursue cross-sectional imaging and an oncology referral to evaluate for pancreatic head malignancy rather than treating for cholelithiasis.
cards.pearl: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder points away from stones and toward malignant obstruction.
cards.explanation: No — this is Courvoisier's sign. Pursue cross-sectional imaging and an oncology referral to evaluate for pancreatic head malignancy rather than treating for cholelithiasis.

cards.title: Beck's triad and tamponade
cards.prompt: A post-MI patient develops JVD, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension. What's your next step?
facts: Get a stat bedside echo to confirm tamponade physiology, then prepare for emergent pericardiocentesis. Don't wait on a formal echo report if the patient is unstable.
cards.pearl: Beck's triad is a call to action, not just a diagnosis to name.
cards.explanation: Get a stat bedside echo to confirm tamponade physiology, then prepare for emergent pericardiocentesis. Don't wait on a formal echo report if the patient is unstable.

cards.title: Pulsus paradoxus
cards.prompt: You measure a 15 mmHg drop in systolic BP with inspiration. What does this change?
facts: Reassess urgently for cardiac tamponade or a severe asthma/COPD exacerbation as the underlying cause, and escalate monitoring and workup accordingly.
cards.pearl: A pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg is a red flag, not an incidental measurement.
cards.explanation: Reassess urgently for cardiac tamponade or a severe asthma/COPD exacerbation as the underlying cause, and escalate monitoring and workup accordingly.

cards.title: Escalating status asthmaticus
cards.prompt: An asthmatic patient is visibly tiring out but sats are still 91%. When do you call anesthesia for possible intubation?
facts: Escalate based on clinical fatigue, a rising CO2, and a quiet chest — not on the pulse oximeter, which can look falsely reassuring right up until a sudden crash.
cards.pearl: In severe asthma, a 'normal' saturation can mask an impending respiratory arrest.
cards.explanation: Escalate based on clinical fatigue, a rising CO2, and a quiet chest — not on the pulse oximeter, which can look falsely reassuring right up until a sudden crash.

cards.title: STEMI activation
cards.prompt: ECG shows ST elevations in II, III, and aVF. What's your immediate priority?
facts: Activate the cath lab immediately and start dual antiplatelet therapy plus anticoagulation per protocol while transport is arranged. Don't delay for troponin results.
cards.pearl: In STEMI, the ECG activates treatment — troponin only confirms it later.
cards.explanation: Activate the cath lab immediately and start dual antiplatelet therapy plus anticoagulation per protocol while transport is arranged. Don't delay for troponin results.

cards.title: Cardiogenic shock after MI
cards.prompt: A post-MI patient becomes hypotensive with cold extremities and a rising lactate. What's your next move?
facts: Start hemodynamic support and urgently involve cardiology for possible mechanical circulatory support, while actively ruling out a mechanical complication like papillary muscle rupture.
cards.pearl: Cardiogenic shock needs a search for a fixable mechanical cause, not just pressor titration.
cards.explanation: Start hemodynamic support and urgently involve cardiology for possible mechanical circulatory support, while actively ruling out a mechanical complication like papillary muscle rupture.

cards.title: Unilateral blown pupil after trauma
cards.prompt: A trauma patient develops a unilateral fixed, dilated pupil. Do you wait for CT confirmation?
facts: No — treat as a neurosurgical emergency, call neurosurgery immediately, and consider hyperosmolar therapy while imaging is being arranged.
cards.pearl: A blown pupil after trauma is uncal herniation until proven otherwise.
cards.explanation: No — treat as a neurosurgical emergency, call neurosurgery immediately, and consider hyperosmolar therapy while imaging is being arranged.

cards.title: Acute stroke, time-critical decisions
cards.prompt: A patient presents with sudden left-sided weakness, last known well 2 hours ago. What's your priority?
facts: Get an emergent non-contrast head CT to rule out hemorrhage and assess thrombolysis eligibility, while simultaneously evaluating for large vessel occlusion and possible thrombectomy.
cards.pearl: In stroke, imaging and treatment decisions happen in parallel, not in sequence.
cards.explanation: Get an emergent non-contrast head CT to rule out hemorrhage and assess thrombolysis eligibility, while simultaneously evaluating for large vessel occlusion and possible thrombectomy.

cards.title: Status epilepticus
cards.prompt: A patient has been seizing continuously for 6 minutes. What's your next step?
facts: Give a benzodiazepine immediately, then move to a second-line agent (e.g., levetiracetam or fosphenytoin) if seizures continue, while securing the airway.
cards.pearl: Seizures past 5 minutes should be treated as status epilepticus — don't wait for a longer cutoff to act.
cards.explanation: Give a benzodiazepine immediately, then move to a second-line agent (e.g., levetiracetam or fosphenytoin) if seizures continue, while securing the airway.

cards.title: Suspected bacterial meningitis
cards.prompt: A patient has fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. Do you wait for the LP before starting antibiotics?
facts: No — draw blood cultures and start empiric antibiotics (plus steroids if indicated) right away. Don't delay treatment for LP or imaging if either will take time.
cards.pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, antibiotics should never wait on the lumbar puncture.
cards.explanation: No — draw blood cultures and start empiric antibiotics (plus steroids if indicated) right away. Don't delay treatment for LP or imaging if either will take time.

cards.title: Cushing's triad
cards.prompt: A patient with a known brain tumor develops worsening headache, vomiting, and bradycardia with hypertension. What are you worried about?
facts: Recognize this as rising intracranial pressure. Elevate the head of bed, consider hyperosmolar therapy, and urgently involve neurosurgery.
cards.pearl: Cushing's triad is a late and ominous sign — don't wait for all three components to act.
cards.explanation: Recognize this as rising intracranial pressure. Elevate the head of bed, consider hyperosmolar therapy, and urgently involve neurosurgery.

cards.title: Fever with relative bradycardia
cards.prompt: A patient has fever, relative bradycardia, and a recent travel history. What do you ask next?
facts: Ask specifically about food and water exposure. Send blood cultures and consider empiric antibiotics for typhoid while results are pending.
cards.pearl: Fever with relative bradycardia (Faget sign) should raise suspicion for typhoid, not just a viral illness.
cards.explanation: Ask specifically about food and water exposure. Send blood cultures and consider empiric antibiotics for typhoid while results are pending.

cards.title: Neutropenic fever
cards.prompt: A chemotherapy patient develops fever with an ANC of 400. What's your next step?
facts: Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour of presentation, without waiting for culture results.
cards.pearl: In neutropenic fever, time to antibiotics is the single biggest driver of outcome.
cards.explanation: Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour of presentation, without waiting for culture results.

cards.title: New murmur, positive blood cultures
cards.prompt: A patient with a new murmur and fever has multiple positive blood cultures. What's your next step?
facts: Obtain an echocardiogram (transthoracic first, transesophageal if inconclusive) and start empiric antibiotics targeting likely organisms while awaiting susceptibilities.
cards.pearl: Persistent bacteremia with a new murmur should prompt an endocarditis work-up, not just repeat cultures.
cards.explanation: Obtain an echocardiogram (transthoracic first, transesophageal if inconclusive) and start empiric antibiotics targeting likely organisms while awaiting susceptibilities.

cards.title: Post-antibiotic diarrhea
cards.prompt: A hospitalized patient develops watery diarrhea after a course of antibiotics. What's your first step?
facts: Send a C. difficile toxin/PCR test, start contact precautions, and begin oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin per severity. Avoid antimotility agents.
cards.pearl: Antimotility agents can worsen C. difficile colitis by trapping toxin in the colon.
cards.explanation: Send a C. difficile toxin/PCR test, start contact precautions, and begin oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin per severity. Avoid antimotility agents.

cards.topic: Diabetic foot ulcer with exposed bone
cards.title: Diabetic foot ulcer with exposed bone
cards.prompt: A diabetic patient has a chronic foot ulcer with exposed bone. Do you need an MRI to confirm osteomyelitis?
facts: A positive probe-to-bone test in a high-risk patient is often enough to start treatment. MRI can confirm if the diagnosis is uncertain or surgical planning is needed.
cards.pearl: If you can probe to bone in a diabetic foot ulcer, treat for osteomyelitis — don't wait on imaging to start care.
cards.explanation: A positive probe-to-bone test in a high-risk patient is often enough to start treatment. MRI can confirm if the diagnosis is uncertain or surgical planning is needed.

cards.title: Acute abdomen triage
cards.prompt: A patient has rebound tenderness, guarding, and rigidity on exam. What's your next step?
facts: Treat this as a surgical abdomen — get surgery involved early and pursue imaging (CT) only if it won't delay definitive care. A peritonitic exam can justify going to the OR before imaging is even back.
cards.pearl: Peritoneal signs are a clinical diagnosis first — don't let imaging delay a surgical consult.
cards.explanation: Treat this as a surgical abdomen — get surgery involved early and pursue imaging (CT) only if it won't delay definitive care. A peritonitic exam can justify going to the OR before imaging is even back.

cards.title: Post-op fever timeline
cards.prompt: A patient spikes a fever on post-op day 3. What's your differential and next step?
facts: Think through the classic post-op fever timeline (atelectasis, UTI, DVT/thrombophlebitis, wound infection, drug fever — the '5 Ws') and target your work-up to day 3, when wound infection and DVT move up the list.
cards.pearl: The post-op day tells you which cause to suspect first, not just a list to run through blindly.
cards.explanation: Think through the classic post-op fever timeline (atelectasis, UTI, DVT/thrombophlebitis, wound infection, drug fever — the '5 Ws') and target your work-up to day 3, when wound infection and DVT move up the list.

cards.title: Compartment syndrome after a fracture
cards.prompt: A patient with a tibia fracture has pain out of proportion to exam and pain with passive stretch. Do you wait for compartment pressure measurements?
facts: No — this is a clinical diagnosis. Loosen constrictive dressings, elevate to heart level (not above), and get orthopedic surgery for emergent fasciotomy without waiting on pressure readings if suspicion is high.
cards.pearl: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch should trigger action before any pressure is measured.
cards.explanation: No — this is a clinical diagnosis. Loosen constrictive dressings, elevate to heart level (not above), and get orthopedic surgery for emergent fasciotomy without waiting on pressure readings if suspicion is high.

cards.title: Anastomotic leak concern
cards.prompt: A patient is tachycardic and has increasing abdominal pain 5 days after a bowel resection. What's your concern?
facts: Suspect an anastomotic leak. Get a CT with oral/rectal contrast, keep the patient NPO, start broad-spectrum antibiotics, and involve surgery urgently — don't wait for a fever to escalate.
cards.pearl: Tachycardia out of proportion to exam findings is often the earliest sign of a leak.
cards.explanation: Suspect an anastomotic leak. Get a CT with oral/rectal contrast, keep the patient NPO, start broad-spectrum antibiotics, and involve surgery urgently — don't wait for a fever to escalate.

cards.topic: Small bowel obstruction, when to operate
cards.title: Small bowel obstruction, when to operate
cards.prompt: A patient with a small bowel obstruction has stable vitals and no peritoneal signs. Do you go straight to the OR?
facts: No — a trial of nasogastric decompression and bowel rest is reasonable first, with serial exams. Peritoneal signs, fever, leukocytosis, or lack of improvement should prompt urgent surgical intervention.
cards.pearl: Not every SBO needs the OR immediately — but a change in exam should change your plan fast.
cards.explanation: No — a trial of nasogastric decompression and bowel rest is reasonable first, with serial exams. Peritoneal signs, fever, leukocytosis, or lack of improvement should prompt urgent surgical intervention.

cards.title: Undifferentiated shock, first move
cards.prompt: A hypotensive patient arrives with an unclear source of shock. What's your first step?
facts: Secure IV access, start fluid resuscitation, and work through the shock categories (hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive) with a rapid bedside exam and point-of-care ultrasound rather than waiting for a full lab panel.
cards.pearl: Treat the physiology while you're still figuring out the diagnosis — resuscitation and work-up happen together.
cards.explanation: Secure IV access, start fluid resuscitation, and work through the shock categories (hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive) with a rapid bedside exam and point-of-care ultrasound rather than waiting for a full lab panel.

cards.title: Chest pain risk stratification
cards.prompt: A patient has atypical chest pain with a normal initial ECG and troponin. Do you send them home?
facts: Not yet — use a validated risk pathway (e.g., HEART score) and consider a repeat troponin before deciding on discharge versus further work-up.
cards.pearl: A single normal troponin doesn't rule out ACS — trending matters more than one value.
cards.explanation: Not yet — use a validated risk pathway (e.g., HEART score) and consider a repeat troponin before deciding on discharge versus further work-up.

cards.title: Anaphylaxis first-line treatment
cards.prompt: A patient develops hives, wheezing, and hypotension after a new medication. What's your first drug?
facts: Intramuscular epinephrine, immediately — not antihistamines or steroids first. Those are adjuncts; epinephrine is the only therapy that reverses the underlying process.
cards.pearl: In anaphylaxis, epinephrine delayed is treatment failed — give it before reaching for anything else.
cards.explanation: Intramuscular epinephrine, immediately — not antihistamines or steroids first. Those are adjuncts; epinephrine is the only therapy that reverses the underlying process.

cards.title: Head injury and anticoagulation
cards.prompt: An elderly patient on apixaban has a minor head strike with a normal initial neuro exam. Do you skip the CT?
facts: No — get a CT head regardless of a reassuring exam. Anticoagulated patients can have a delayed or occult intracranial bleed even when they look fine initially.
cards.pearl: A normal neuro exam doesn't clear an anticoagulated head injury — imaging is not optional here.
cards.explanation: No — get a CT head regardless of a reassuring exam. Anticoagulated patients can have a delayed or occult intracranial bleed even when they look fine initially.

cards.title: Sepsis bundle timing
cards.prompt: A patient meets criteria for sepsis with a lactate of 4. What's your priority in the first hour?
facts: Draw blood cultures before antibiotics if it won't cause delay, then start broad-spectrum antibiotics and begin fluid resuscitation — all within the first hour, not sequentially over several hours.
cards.pearl: In sepsis, the clock starts at recognition — every hour of delayed antibiotics measurably worsens outcomes.
cards.explanation: Draw blood cultures before antibiotics if it won't cause delay, then start broad-spectrum antibiotics and begin fluid resuscitation — all within the first hour, not sequentially over several hours.
